questions.sec: MMSE and frontal-lobe surface orientation
questions.q: What is the stated purpose of the mini-mental state examination (MMSE)?
opts: To localise a visual-field defect without cognitive testing
To measure cerebellar coordination alone
To assess higher mental functions and cognitive status
To grade isolated lower-motor-neuron weakness
questions.exp: The MMSE is introduced as helping to assess higher mental functions and cognitive status. (Book p555)

questions.sec: MMSE and frontal-lobe surface orientation
questions.q: The page's ORARLC mnemonic for MMSE is expanded as which sequence?
opts: Orientation, reflexes, attention, reading, language and calculation
Observation, registration, arousal, recall, localisation and copying
Orientation, registration, arithmetic, reasoning, language and coordination
Orientation, registration, attention, recall, language and copying
questions.exp: The printed MMSE list is ORARLC: orientation, registration, attention, recall, language and copying. (Book p555)

questions.sec: MMSE and frontal-lobe surface orientation
questions.q: On the superolateral surface diagram, a lesion immediately posterior to the central sulcus lies in which labelled lobe?
opts: Parietal lobe
Temporal lobe
Occipital lobe
Frontal lobe
questions.exp: The superolateral diagram places the parietal lobe posterior to the central sulcus and the frontal lobe anterior to it. (Book p555)

questions.sec: MMSE and frontal-lobe surface orientation
questions.q: Which map relationship is represented by the Sylvian fissure label?
opts: It is the groove between the precentral and postcentral gyri
It forms the lateral boundary around the frontal and temporal regions on the superolateral surface
It separates the occipital lobe from the cerebellum
It marks the medial boundary between the two hemispheres
questions.exp: The superolateral surface labels the Sylvian fissure laterally, with frontal and temporal regions around it; the central sulcus is the separate motor-sensory landmark. (Book p555)

questions.sec: MMSE and frontal-lobe surface orientation
questions.q: Which cortex-to-lobe pairing agrees with the lower functional map?
opts: Motor cortex—temporal; somatosensory—occipital; auditory—parietal; visual—frontal
All four cortices are labelled inside the frontal lobe
Motor cortex—frontal; somatosensory cortex—parietal; auditory cortex—temporal; visual cortex—occipital
Motor cortex—occipital; somatosensory—temporal; auditory—frontal; visual—parietal
questions.exp: The lower diagram labels motor cortex in the frontal region, somatosensory cortex in the parietal region, auditory cortex in the temporal region and visual cortex in the occipital region. (Book p555)

questions.sec: Frontal-lobe areas and surface anatomy
questions.q: A functional map labels the precentral gyrus as which Brodmann area and role?
opts: Area 6, the premotor area
Area 8, the frontal eye field
Areas 44 and 45, Broca's motor speech area
Area 4, the primary motor area
questions.exp: The map labels area 4 in the precentral gyrus as the primary motor area. (Book p556)

questions.sec: Frontal-lobe areas and surface anatomy
questions.q: Which area-function pairing is printed for the premotor and supplementary motor regions?
opts: Area 6—premotor area; area 8—supplementary motor area medially
Area 4—supplementary motor area; area 6—primary sensory area
Area 8—Broca area; areas 44 and 45—frontal eye field
Areas 9–12—premotor area; area 6—prefrontal pole
questions.exp: The functional map identifies area 6 as premotor and area 8 as supplementary motor area medially; it separately labels another area-8 region as the frontal eye field. (Book p556)

questions.sec: Frontal-lobe areas and surface anatomy
questions.q: Which label is assigned to the area-8 region on the frontal-lobe map besides the supplementary motor area?
opts: Parieto-occipital association area
Frontal eye field
Primary auditory cortex
Angular gyrus
questions.exp: Area 8 is also labelled the frontal eye field on the functional frontal-lobe diagram. (Book p556)

questions.sec: Frontal-lobe areas and surface anatomy
questions.q: Which set and position are printed for the prefrontal area?
opts: Areas 44 and 45, inside the precentral gyrus
Areas 17 and 18, inferior to the Sylvian fissure
Areas 9, 10, 11 and 12, anterior to areas 6 and 8
Areas 1, 2 and 3, posterior to the central sulcus
questions.exp: The map gives the prefrontal area as areas 9, 10, 11 and 12, anterior to areas 6 and 8. (Book p556)

questions.sec: Frontal-lobe areas and surface anatomy
questions.q: A lesion of the inferior frontal gyrus is being correlated with the speech label on the diagram. Which area is implicated?
opts: Area 4, the precentral motor area
Area 22, the auditory comprehension area
Area 17, the primary visual area
Areas 44 and 45, the motor speech area of Broca
questions.exp: The diagram places the motor speech area of Broca in the inferior frontal gyrus and labels it areas 44 and 45. (Book p556)

questions.sec: Frontal-lobe areas and surface anatomy
questions.q: Which collection belongs to the medial-surface diagram rather than the inferior-surface diagram?
opts: Cingulate gyrus and sulcus, paracentral lobule, corpus callosum, fornix, hippocampal gyrus and uncus
Rectus gyrus, olfactory sulcus and H-shaped orbital sulcus
Precentral gyrus, postcentral gyrus and central sulcus
Lateral orbital gyrus, posterior orbital gyrus and orbital sulcus only
questions.exp: The medial-surface drawing labels the paracentral lobule, superior frontal and cingulate gyri/sulcus, corpus callosum, fornix, hippocampal gyrus and uncus, along with posterior medial structures. The inferior drawing carries the orbital and olfactory labels. (Book p556)

questions.sec: Frontal-lobe areas and surface anatomy
questions.q: What landmark and arrangement are shown on the inferior surface of the frontal lobe?
opts: The hippocampal sulcus surrounding the corpus callosum
The olfactory sulcus beside the rectus gyrus and an H-shaped orbital sulcus dividing orbital gyri
The calcarine fissure dividing the cuneus from the lingual gyrus
The central sulcus dividing motor from sensory cortex
questions.exp: The inferior-surface diagram labels the olfactory sulcus beside the rectus gyrus and the orbital sulcus as H shaped, with anterior, medial, lateral and posterior orbital gyri around it. (Book p556)

questions.sec: Motor cortex, movement sequence and homunculus
questions.q: What proportion of motor fibres is printed as originating from area 4, and what is special about its Betz cells?
opts: Only 5%; Betz cells are sensory relay cells with the highest threshold
All motor fibres; Betz cells are cerebellar Purkinje cells
Only 30%; Betz cells are specialised and have the lowest threshold to initiate motor activity
About 70%; Betz cells inhibit all motor activity
questions.exp: For area 4/primary motor cortex/precentral gyrus, the page states that only 30% of motor fibres originate there and that specialised Betz cells have the lowest threshold to initiate motor activity. (Book p557)

questions.sec: Motor cortex, movement sequence and homunculus
questions.q: Damage confined to area 4 would most directly disrupt which printed function?
opts: The sensory guidance formula for a learned action only
Reward-based behavioural response without weakness
Visual recognition of an object by touch
Initiation of fine skilled voluntary movement
questions.exp: Area 4 is stated to initiate fine skilled voluntary movement; preparation and finesse are assigned to other parts of the sequence. (Book p557)

questions.sec: Motor cortex, movement sequence and homunculus
questions.q: What is the role of the premotor area (PMA) and supplementary motor area (SMA) in the printed movement model?
opts: They provide 30% of motor fibres and prepare movement through postural tone, proximal alignment and antagonist inhibition
They provide all motor fibres and perform only cerebellar finesse
They receive visual input and perform language comprehension
They initiate movement but do not influence posture or antagonists
questions.exp: PMA and SMA are stated to provide 30% of motor fibres and prepare fine skilled voluntary movement by setting tone of posture, proximal muscle alignment and antagonist muscle inhibition. (Book p557)

questions.sec: Motor cortex, movement sequence and homunculus
questions.q: A bilateral PMA/SMA lesion is expected, according to the page, to produce which pair?
opts: Akinetic mutism and alexia without agraphia
Spasticity from a tone disturbance and primitive reflexes
Flaccidity and loss of all primitive reflexes
Pure sensory ataxia and visual agnosia
questions.exp: The page notes that bilateral PMA/SMA lesions cause spasticity (a tone issue) and primitive reflexes. (Book p557)

questions.sec: Motor cortex, movement sequence and homunculus
questions.q: Which ordered chain follows the printed process of fine-skilled voluntary movement?
opts: Planning by PMA/SMA → preparation by basal ganglia → initiation by cerebellum → finesse by primary motor area
Planning by primary motor area → preparation by cerebellum → initiation by PMA/SMA → finesse by basal ganglia
Planning and coordination by basal ganglia → preparation by PMA/SMA → initiation by primary motor area → finesse by cerebellum
Planning by cerebellum → preparation by primary motor area → initiation by basal ganglia → finesse by PMA/SMA
questions.exp: The note orders fine-skilled movement as planning and coordination by the basal ganglia, preparation or setting up by PMA/SMA, initiation by the primary motor area, and finesse by the cerebellum. (Book p557)

questions.sec: Motor cortex, movement sequence and homunculus
questions.q: Which vascular distribution matches the motor homunculus labels?
opts: Lower limb on the superolateral surface is supplied by MCA; face and upper limb medially by ACA
All face, upper-limb and lower-limb representations are supplied by ACA
The face is supplied by PCA while the lower limb is supplied by MCA
Lower limb on the medial surface is supplied by ACA; face and upper limb on the superolateral surface are supplied by MCA
questions.exp: The motor homunculus note assigns the lower limb to the medial surface and ACA, while face and upper limb lie on the superolateral surface and are supplied by MCA. (Book p557)

questions.sec: Motor cortex, movement sequence and homunculus
questions.q: Why can a cortical vascular lesion produce face/upper-limb-predominant versus lower-limb-predominant weakness?
opts: The motor homunculus places the lower limb medially and the face and upper limb superolaterally, so the affected vessel and side determine the pattern
The cerebellum reverses the body map in every cortical lesion
The frontal eye field supplies the lower limb but not the face
The parietal lobe contains no somatotopic motor representation
questions.exp: The page links the weakness pattern to the motor homunculus: lower limb is medial/ACA territory, while face and upper limb are superolateral/MCA territory. (Book p557)

questions.sec: Motor lesions, frontal eye field and Broca area
questions.q: A patient has face and upper-limb weakness after a cortical lesion. Which territory is the page's best fit?
opts: PPRF territory in the brainstem
MCA territory
ACA territory affecting the medial paracentral lobule
PCA territory affecting the occipital cortex
questions.exp: The page states MCA lesion causes face and upper-limb weakness, while ACA lesion causes lower-limb weakness with urinary incontinence. (Book p558)

questions.sec: Motor lesions, frontal eye field and Broca area
questions.q: Which presentation is paired with an ACA lesion on the page?
opts: Contralateral homonymous hemianopia from the occipital pole
Ipsilateral gaze paralysis from a PPRF lesion
Lower-limb weakness with urinary incontinence from paracentral-lobule involvement on the medial surface
Face and upper-limb weakness with spared bladder function
questions.exp: An ACA lesion is printed as producing lower-limb weakness plus urinary incontinence, attributed to the paracentral lobule on the medial surface. (Book p558)

questions.sec: Motor lesions, frontal eye field and Broca area
questions.q: What is the characteristic motor-cortex lesion pattern described?
opts: Ipsilateral flaccid weakness with isolated loss of vibration
Bilateral weakness with normal tone and no motor deficit
Pure aphasia without any contralateral motor involvement
Contralateral weakness of fine skilled voluntary movement with an UMN pattern of spasticity or hypertonia
questions.exp: A motor-cortex lesion is described as contralateral weakness of fine skilled voluntary movements and an UMN lesion with spasticity or hypertonia. (Book p558)

questions.sec: Motor lesions, frontal eye field and Broca area
questions.q: An irritative motor-cortex lesion produces repeated spreading contractions beginning in one body part. Which label is printed?
opts: A contralateral motor simple partial seizure with Jacksonian march
An ipsilateral absence seizure with no motor spread
A cerebellar intention tremor with dysmetria
A lower-motor-neuron fasciculation with muscle wasting
questions.exp: The irritative lesion line states that a contralateral motor simple partial seizure may occur, with Jacksonian march. (Book p558)

questions.sec: Motor lesions, frontal eye field and Broca area
questions.q: The page defines the upper motor neuron (UMN) span as extending from where to where?
opts: From the retina to the superior colliculus
From the cortex to the anterior horn cell in grey matter
From the anterior horn cell to the neuromuscular junction
From the cerebellum to the dorsal-root ganglion
questions.exp: The printed definition says UMN runs from the cortex till the anterior horn cell, which is in grey matter. (Book p558)

questions.sec: Motor lesions, frontal eye field and Broca area
questions.q: In the frontal-eye-field circuit, what do PPRF, LR, MR and MLF stand for?
opts: Primary pontine reflex field; lateral rotation; motor rotation; midline longitudinal fibre
Posterior parietal reticular formation; levator rectus; motor rectus; main lateral fasciculus
Paramedian pontine reticular formation; lateral rectus; medial rectus; medial longitudinal fasciculus
Parietal pontine relay formation; longus rectus; middle rectus; medial limbic fibre
questions.exp: The abbreviations printed beside the FEF diagram are PPRF—parapontine reticular formation, LR—lateral rectus, MR—medial rectus and MLF—medial longitudinal fasciculus. (Book p558)

questions.sec: Motor lesions, frontal eye field and Broca area
questions.q: The left frontal eye field normally activates which muscles to make the eyes look right?
opts: Left lateral rectus and right medial rectus
Both medial recti only
Both lateral recti only
Right lateral rectus and left medial rectus
questions.exp: The diagram states that the left FEF activates the right lateral rectus and left medial rectus, producing rightward gaze. (Book p558)

questions.sec: Motor lesions, frontal eye field and Broca area
questions.q: A left frontal-lobe FEF lesion is shown on examination. What gaze position is printed?
opts: The patient looks toward the left, the side of the lesion; a brainstem PPRF lesion makes the patient look away from its side
The patient looks right, away from the cortical lesion; a PPRF lesion looks toward its side
The eyes remain fixed centrally in both lesions
The patient looks up in the cortical lesion and down in the PPRF lesion
questions.exp: The page states that a left FEF lesion prevents rightward gaze, so the patient looks left, toward the lesion. A brainstem PPRF lesion causes looking away from the side of the lesion. (Book p558)

questions.sec: Motor lesions, frontal eye field and Broca area
questions.q: Which language deficit and anatomical comparison are paired with Broca's area on the page?
opts: Area 4 injury causes fluent jargon; all posterior lesions cause dysarthria
Area 44/45 injury causes non-fluent aphasia; anterior-central-sulcus lesions affect fluency, whereas posterior lesions affect comprehension
Area 22 injury causes non-fluent aphasia; posterior lesions affect fluency and anterior lesions comprehension
Area 17 injury causes alexia; central-sulcus lesions spare both fluency and comprehension
questions.exp: Broca's area/areas 44 and 45 are linked to impaired fluency or non-fluent aphasia. The note contrasts anterior-to-central-sulcus lesions affecting fluency with posterior-to-central-sulcus lesions affecting comprehension. (Book p558)

questions.sec: Prefrontal cortex and bilateral frontal pathology
questions.q: Which prefrontal-part to function table is printed?
opts: Dorsolateral PFC—language comprehension; medial PFC—touch; orbital PFC—smell; frontal pole—pain
All four PFC parts are assigned the same executive function
Dorsolateral PFC—executive function; medial PFC/cingulate—emotion and motivation; orbital PFC—behavioural response; frontal pole—theory of mind
Dorsolateral PFC—vision; medial PFC—hearing; orbital PFC—fine movement; frontal pole—balance
questions.exp: The table pairs dorsolateral PFC with executive function, medial PFC or cingulate gyrus with emotion and motivation, orbital PFC with behavioural response, and frontal pole with theory of mind. (Book p559)

questions.sec: Prefrontal cortex and bilateral frontal pathology
questions.q: A patient cannot suppress a prepotent response and cannot flexibly shift between task sets. Which printed executive domain is affected?
opts: Theory of mind involving only empathy
Motor initiation involving only Betz cells
Visual agnosia involving the supramarginal gyrus
Timeframe-dependent, goal-directed executive function involving cognitive inhibition, response inhibition and set shifting
questions.exp: Executive function is described as timeframe-dependent, goal-directed activity with cognitive inhibition, response inhibition and set shifting or flexibility. (Book p559)

questions.sec: Prefrontal cortex and bilateral frontal pathology
questions.q: The page orders loss of energisation and motivation from mild to severe as:
opts: Apathy → abulia → akinetic mutism
Abulia → apathy → akinetic mutism
Akinetic mutism → apathy → abulia
Apathy → akinetic mutism → abulia
questions.exp: The printed severity sequence is apathy when mild, then abulia, then akinetic mutism when severe. (Book p559)

questions.sec: Prefrontal cortex and bilateral frontal pathology
questions.q: Behavioural response in the prefrontal table is based on what, and what does the JIPFA list include?
opts: Tone and posture; proximal alignment, antagonist inhibition, gait and balance
Reward and punishment; judgement, insight, problem solving/personality, fluency and abstract thinking
Pain and temperature; jaw, intention, proprioception, fine touch and ataxia
Sleep and arousal; memory, orientation, registration, language and copying
questions.exp: Behavioural response is based on reward and punishment and includes JIPFA: judgement, insight, problem solving/personality, fluency and abstract thinking. (Book p559)

questions.sec: Prefrontal cortex and bilateral frontal pathology
questions.q: Which statement best reflects the page's theory-of-mind line?
opts: It means initiating eye movements, while metacognition means inhibiting reflexes
It is the same as motor finesse, while metacognition means calculating a percentage
It includes sympathy and empathy, while metacognition means understanding oneself
It is limited to writing and naming, while metacognition means recognising objects by touch
questions.exp: Theory of mind is listed with sympathy and empathy; metacognition is defined on the page as understanding oneself. (Book p559)

questions.sec: Prefrontal cortex and bilateral frontal pathology
questions.q: Which cluster is the page's bilateral frontal-lobe pathology list?
opts: Isolated anosmia, homonymous hemianopia, pure alexia and dysmetria
Fluent aphasia, inferior quadrantanopia, facial palsy and sensory extinction
Rest tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia and levodopa-induced dyskinesia
Prefrontal personality change, urinary incontinence from bilateral paracentral lesions, primitive reflexes from premotor involvement, akinetic mutism and gait apraxia in NPH
questions.exp: The bilateral frontal pathology list contains prefrontal personality changes, urinary incontinence due to bilateral paracentral-lobule lesions, primitive reflexes due to premotor-cortex involvement, akinetic mutism as severe apathy and gait apraxia in normal-pressure hydrocephalus. (Book p559)

questions.sec: Prefrontal cortex and bilateral frontal pathology
questions.q: A patient with normal-pressure hydrocephalus has gait apraxia and says the foot feels stuck to the floor. Which mechanism phrase is printed?
opts: Ignition failure
Loss of visual object recognition
Disconnection between visual cortices
Failure of the lateral rectus to abduct
questions.exp: Gait apraxia is associated with normal-pressure hydrocephalus and is described as ignition failure, with the foot feeling stuck to the floor. (Book p559)

units.title: 1. MMSE and frontal-lobe surface orientation
units.guide:
The page opens with the MMSE and its ORARLC components.
The superolateral maps orient the frontal lobe against the central sulcus, parietal, temporal and occipital lobes, while the cortex map identifies motor, somatosensory, auditory and visual regions.

units.title: 2. Frontal-lobe areas and surface anatomy
units.guide:
Area 4, area 6, the two area-8 labels, prefrontal areas 9–12 and Broca areas 44–45 are read from the functional map.
The medial-surface and inferior-surface diagrams retain their named gyri, sulci and fissures, including the H-shaped orbital sulcus.

units.title: 3. Motor cortex, movement sequence and homunculus
units.sec: Motor cortex, movement sequence and homunculus
units.guide:
Primary motor cortex, Betz cells, premotor/supplementary preparation and bilateral-lesion findings are kept in sequence.
The fine-skilled movement chain and the medial-versus-superolateral motor homunculus supply are then tested as a functional whole.

units.title: 4. Motor lesions, frontal eye field and Broca area
units.sec: Motor lesions, frontal eye field and Broca area
units.guide:
The page applies ACA/MCA territory to weakness and incontinence, then distinguishes motor-cortex and irritative lesions.
The frontal-eye-field circuit, gaze deviation rules, Broca area and the anterior/posterior central-sulcus note close the motor section.

units.title: 5. Prefrontal cortex and bilateral frontal pathology
units.sec: Prefrontal cortex and bilateral frontal pathology
units.guide:
Areas 9–12 are divided into dorsolateral, medial/cingulate, orbital and frontal-pole functions.
Executive function, motivation, reward-based behaviour, theory of mind and the bilateral frontal pathology list are kept in the printed order.
